title: Conjunctive queries: syntax and semantics
lead: Relational calculus, CQ rules, substitutions, homomorphisms and query answers.

sections.title: Algebra and declarative query languages
sections.html:
Relational algebra gives an operational expression using selection, projection and joins. Relational calculus describes output values using logical formulas. The DBMS translates a declarative query into a plan that can be optimised and executed.

The source database has Flight(origin, destination, airline) and Airport(code, city). Projection retrieves airlines; selection and projection retrieve London airport codes; joining two renamed Airport references with Flight identifies direct flights between specified cities.

Conjunctive queries capture the selection/projection/join fragment under set semantics. Their logical form uses conjunction and existential quantification, without negation or disjunction in the basic language.

PDF pp. 1–14

sections.title: CQ syntax: head and body
sections.html:
Write a CQ as Q(x) :- R₁(v₁), …, Rₘ(vₘ). The head lists distinguished/output variables. The body is a conjunction of relational atoms. Variables used only in the body are existentially quantified.

An atom names a relation and gives a term for each attribute position. Terms can be variables or constants. Reusing a variable requires the same value in every occurrence, so repeated variables express equality constraints.

Output variables must occur in the body for the range-restricted queries considered here. A Boolean CQ has no output variables and asks whether any assignment satisfies the body. Constants retain their specified values.

PDF pp. 15–19

sections.title: The Flight/Airport source query
sections.html:
The source expresses direct airlines from London to Glasgow as Q(z) :- Airport(x,London), Airport(y,Glasgow), Flight(x,y,z). London and Glasgow are constants; x and y are existential variables; z is the output variable.

An answer needs an origin airport in London, a destination airport in Glasgow and a Flight tuple connecting those same codes. Finding one atom independently is insufficient: shared variables must agree across all atoms.

The listed data contains Airport(LGW,London), Airport(GLA,Glasgow) and Flight(LGW,GLA,U2). They support the output U2. The result is a set, so several supporting flights with the same airline would not duplicate that airline in the answer.

PDF pp. 20–25

sections.title: Substitutions and homomorphisms
sections.html:
A substitution maps terms to terms. A homomorphism h from atom set A to atom set B fixes every constant and maps every atom of A into an atom present in B. The same mapping is used for every occurrence of a variable.

To check a proposed mapping, replace every argument in each source atom and test membership of the resulting atom in the target. Relation names and argument positions are preserved.

Different source variables may map to the same target value: a homomorphism need not be injective. It also need not cover every target atom. These properties distinguish pattern matching from a one-to-one correspondence between entire databases.

PDF pp. 26–30

sections.title: Semantics of a CQ answer
sections.html:
A match of Q in database D is a homomorphism from Q’s body to D. For each match h, output the head tuple h(x). Thus Q(D) = {h(x) | h(body) ⊆ D}, with constants fixed.

For the source flight query, h(x) = LGW, h(y) = GLA and h(z) = U2 satisfies all three atoms, giving the output tuple (U2). Values for existential variables are witnesses rather than additional output columns.

Several matches can yield the same output tuple, which appears once under set semantics. Evaluating the query means finding whether matches exist and collecting their head values.

PDF pp. 31–33

quiz.question: In Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(y), what is y?
options: An existentially quantified variable shared by the two atoms
quiz.explanation: The variable y does not appear in the head, but every occurrence of y must receive the same value within an assignment.

source.summary: Lecture 23 connects relational algebra and calculus with conjunctive queries. It defines head and body syntax, homomorphisms, and result semantics in terms of matches.
